items.original_title: FinancialJuice: ING: Don't Call it a Dollar Comeback

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: ING: Don't Call it a Dollar Comeback
evidence.snippet: The Fed decision remains a close call, but the base case now favours a rate hike later this month. A bearish flattening of the US yield curve would typically support the dollar, especially against lower-yielding currencies, leading to a revised year-end EUR/USD forecast of around 1.16 from 1.18 previously. Even so, this is not viewed as the start of a major tightening cycle, and the expected cyclical dollar decline is delayed rather than cancelled. That weaker-dollar move is now pushed back to next spring, when inflation is expected to be closer to 2% and markets may begin pricing policy normalisation toward 3.25%. USD/JPY is still seen more likely in a 155-160 range than below 150, despite faster BoJ tightening expectations. Elsewhere, higher rates should support the Australian dollar and Norwegian krone, while the Swiss franc may stay under pressure. High-yielding EM currencies are also expected to remain favoured in a relatively low-volatility environment.

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Goldman Sachs: Yen Strength, Energy Risk and AI Momentum Drive Markets
evidence.snippet: Asian technology and semiconductor stocks rallied as GPT-6 momentum continued, with SoftBank up roughly 30% in three days. The bigger surprise was the yen’s sharp appreciation after stronger Japanese wage data reinforced expectations for further BoJ tightening. That raises fresh questions around a potential yen carry-trade unwind and the implications for global equities and credit, while Japanese exporters are underperforming as they face both a stronger currency and higher energy costs. Energy remains the clearest near-term risk to equities. Iran’s proposed exclusion zone could further restrict ship-to-ship transfers, while Hormuz flows are still only around 10mb/d and refined-product markets remain tight. There is some optimism around diplomacy as Iran says talks with Oman are nearing agreement, but there is still no operational solution or broader US deal. Russia-Ukraine tensions are also adding risk for Europe, while copper continues to make new LME highs despite stagflation concerns, reflecting supply constraints, tariff distortions and still-strong spending rather than a pure growth signal.

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Credit Agricole: EU-China Trade Imbalance and Strategic Dependence Are Deepening
evidence.snippet: China’s trade surplus with the EU continues to widen as Chinese manufactured exports grow faster than European exports to China. The largest imbalances are concentrated in electrical equipment, machinery, automobiles and e-commerce-related goods. At the same time, the EU is becoming more dependent on China for critical minerals, batteries, magnets, solar products and other strategic inputs, raising economic-security concerns. The likely response is a mix of dialogue, targeted trade-defence measures, procurement rules and supply-chain resilience policies, but China retains significant capacity to retaliate through export controls and restrictions on commercial cooperation, increasing the risk of further trade tensions.
